subtopic_detail: Managing severe obstructive sleep apnoea in a commercial vehicle driver
stem:
A 52-year-old man attends your general practice for the results of a sleep study. He drives a public route bus 5 days a week and holds a commercial vehicle licence.

His wife has complained for years about his snoring and has watched him stop breathing and then gasp. He tells you, once you ask directly, that he has twice nodded off while stopped at traffic lights during his shift, and that he drinks energy drinks to get through the afternoon run.

His body mass index is 34 and his blood pressure today is 152/92 mmHg on no antihypertensive. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. Laboratory polysomnography reports an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 32 events per hour with a minimum oxygen saturation of 84 per cent and no central events. His thyroid function is normal and his haemoglobin is 158 g/L (130-180). He asks what this means for his job.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 152/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Polysomnography apnoea-hypopnoea index 32 events per hour, minimum SpO2 84%, no central events; Epworth Sleepiness Scale 17 out of 24; thyroid function normal; haemoglobin 158 g/L (130-180)
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34, crowded oropharynx, no goitre

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure and advise that he must notify the licensing authority
options.rationale: An apnoea-hypopnoea index above 30 with excessive daytime sleepiness and episodes of falling asleep at the wheel is severe obstructive sleep apnoea, which under the Australian fitness to drive standard makes a person not fit to hold a commercial licence until effectively treated. Continuous positive airway pressure is first line for severe disease, and the licence holder carries a legal duty to report the condition to the driver licensing authority. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement

options.text: Fit a mandibular advancement splint and review his daytime sleepiness in 3 months
options.rationale: Oral appliances are an accepted option for mild to moderate disease or where continuous positive airway pressure is not tolerated, but they achieve lower and less predictable reductions in the apnoea-hypopnoea index than is needed for severe disease in a commercial driver. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement

options.text: Recommend a structured weight loss programme and repeat the sleep study in 6 months
options.rationale: Weight loss is an essential parallel intervention and can substantially reduce the apnoea-hypopnoea index, but it takes months, and leaving him driving a bus untreated in the meantime is the central problem with this option. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive

options.text: Start modafinil for his daytime sleepiness and review his Epworth score in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Wake-promoting agents are reserved for residual sleepiness that persists despite adequate continuous positive airway pressure use, and using one to mask sleepiness in an untreated driver removes his warning symptom without treating the apnoea. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement

options.text: Refer for uvulopalatopharyngoplasty and review his sleep study 3 months after surgery
options.rationale: Upper airway surgery has modest and unpredictable success rates in severe obstructive sleep apnoea and is considered only after continuous positive airway pressure has genuinely failed or been rejected. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea is graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index as mild at 5 to 15, moderate at 15 to 30 and severe above 30 events per hour, but the management decision depends on symptoms and risk as much as on the number. Continuous positive airway pressure is first line for severe disease and for symptomatic moderate disease, with oral appliances, weight loss, positional therapy and surgery occupying defined secondary roles. The occupational dimension is what raises the stakes here: the Australian fitness to drive standard treats severe obstructive sleep apnoea with excessive sleepiness as incompatible with a commercial licence until treated, and a history of falling asleep at the wheel is regarded as a particularly serious indicator. Licence holders have a legal obligation to report a condition likely to affect safe driving, and treating clinicians should document that this advice was given. Untreated disease also contributes to resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation and stroke risk, so the cardiovascular consequences are treated as part of the same problem.
key_points: An apnoea-hypopnoea index above 30 defines severe disease; continuous positive airway pressure is first line
Severe disease with excessive sleepiness makes a driver unfit for a commercial licence until effectively treated
Falling asleep at the wheel is a particularly serious indicator and should be asked about directly
Oral appliances, weight loss and surgery have defined secondary roles rather than first-line status
Wake-promoting agents are only for residual sleepiness despite adequate treatment
explanation.pearls: Commercial drivers on continuous positive airway pressure generally require documented adherence, conventionally at least 4 hours per night on 70 per cent of nights, before conditional fitness is granted, and downloaded machine data rather than self-report is what the licensing authority accepts.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Obstructive sleep apnoea position statement

subtopic_detail: Management of acute bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with erythema nodosum and ankle arthritis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends your general practice with 3 weeks of painful red raised lumps on both shins and 10 days of painful, swollen ankles that make walking to the bus difficult.

She has also had a dry cough and has felt feverish in the evenings. She has no weight loss, no night sweats and no haemoptysis. She has never smoked, has had no overseas travel, and has had no contact with anyone with a chronic cough.

On examination there are tender erythematous nodules over both shins and warm, swollen, tender ankles bilaterally. Her chest is clear on auscultation, her eyes are not red and there is no rash elsewhere.

Her chest radiograph reports symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. Her corrected calcium is 2.40 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), C-reactive protein 48 mg/L (less than 5), angiotensin converting enzyme is raised, and her full blood count, renal function and liver function are within normal limits. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay is negative, her antistreptolysin O titre is not raised and a pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Tender erythematous nodules over both shins, warm swollen tender ankles bilaterally, clear chest, no ocular redness
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), C-reactive protein 48 mg/L (less than 5), raised angiotensin converting enzyme, full blood count renal and liver function within normal limits, QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus negative, antistreptolysin O not raised, pregnancy test negative
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph with symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and clear lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for endobronchial ultrasound guided biopsy of the mediastinal lymph nodes
options.rationale: Tissue confirmation is required where the presentation is atypical or malignancy is a concern, but this triad is sufficiently characteristic that Australian and international guidance accepts a clinical diagnosis without biopsy. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources

options.text: Symptomatic treatment with naproxen and clinical review with repeat imaging in 6 weeks
options.rationale: The combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral ankle arthritis and symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy describes an acute sarcoid presentation that remits spontaneously in the great majority of cases within 6 to 24 months, so non-steroidal anti-inflammatory treatment with follow-up is sufficient. Corticosteroids and biopsy are both reserved for atypical features or organ-threatening disease. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources
Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

options.text: Prednisolone 25 mg daily for 6 weeks with a tapering plan and bone protection advice
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are indicated for cardiac, neurological or ocular sarcoidosis, hypercalcaemia or progressive pulmonary disease, none of which is present, and they would expose her to steroid toxicity for a self-limiting syndrome. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources

options.text: Start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for presumed tuberculous adenitis
options.rationale: Tuberculous mediastinal lymphadenopathy is usually asymmetrical and is accompanied by constitutional symptoms, and a negative interferon gamma release assay with no exposure history makes it unlikely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Start weekly methotrexate with folic acid and arrange rheumatology review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing agent for chronic or refractory sarcoidosis, so introducing it at first presentation of a self-limiting syndrome inverts the treatment sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause that most often presents in adults between 20 and 40, and its acute form carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous remission in most patients. The characteristic acute triad of erythema nodosum, bilateral ankle arthritis and symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, often accompanied by fever, is distinctive enough that tissue confirmation is not required. Serum angiotensin converting enzyme is neither sensitive nor specific and should not be used to make or exclude the diagnosis. The features that do change management are hypercalcaemia from unregulated conversion of vitamin D by granulomas, cardiac involvement with conduction disease or arrhythmia, neurological involvement, and eye disease, so ocular review, an electrocardiogram and a calcium level are part of the initial assessment of anyone with sarcoidosis. Treatment is reserved for organ-threatening or progressive disease.
key_points: Erythema nodosum with bilateral ankle arthritis and symmetrical hilar lymphadenopathy allows a clinical diagnosis without biopsy
The acute form remits spontaneously in most patients within 6 to 24 months
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory treatment with follow-up is the appropriate first management
Corticosteroids are reserved for cardiac, neurological, ocular, hypercalcaemic or progressive pulmonary disease
Angiotensin converting enzyme level is neither sensitive nor specific and does not establish the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Every patient with newly diagnosed sarcoidosis needs an electrocardiogram, a calcium level and an ophthalmology review, because cardiac, hypercalcaemic and ocular involvement can be silent yet are the three that most often demand corticosteroid therapy.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis clinical resources

subtopic_detail: Investigating macrocytic anaemia with dysplastic neutrophils and normal haematinics in an older adult
stem:
You are the medical registrar in an outpatient clinic. A 73-year-old man is referred with 4 months of tiredness that has stopped him playing bowls, and two falls that he attributes to feeling lightheaded when he stands.

He has had no bleeding from any site, no black stools and no weight loss. He drinks one glass of wine a week, takes no regular medications and has had no recent infections or travel.

His haemoglobin is 92 g/L (130-180) with a mean corpuscular volume of 106 fL (80-100), white cell count 3.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), and platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400). His reticulocyte count is 22 x10^9/L (20-100) and his lactate dehydrogenase is within normal limits. Serum vitamin B12, red cell folate, thyroid stimulating hormone, renal function and liver function are all within normal limits. The blood film is reported as showing hypogranular neutrophils, several with bilobed nuclei, and no circulating blasts. Examination finds no lymphadenopathy, no splenomegaly and no petechiae.

data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (130-180), mean corpuscular volume 106 fL (80-100), white cell count 3.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), reticulocytes 22 x10^9/L (20-100), lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, vitamin B12 red cell folate thyroid renal and liver function all within normal limits
data_table.Blood film: Hypogranular neutrophils with several bilobed forms, no circulating blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells and repeat the full blood count in 3 months
options.rationale: Transfusion treats the symptom while leaving a trilineage marrow disorder undiagnosed, and repeated transfusion without a diagnosis leads to iron loading and alloimmunisation. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources

options.text: Start oral folic acid with an empirical vitamin B12 injection and repeat the count in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Both haematinics are already documented as normal, so replacing them treats a deficiency that has been excluded and delays the diagnosis by 6 weeks. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources

options.text: Refer for bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetic and molecular studies
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with a raised mean corpuscular volume, an inadequate reticulocyte response and hypogranular bilobed neutrophils on the film is dysplasia, and normal haematinics with normal thyroid, renal and liver function remove the reversible explanations. Marrow examination with cytogenetics and molecular testing is required both to confirm myelodysplasia and to assign the prognostic score that drives treatment. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources
Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology

options.text: Start a subcutaneous erythropoiesis stimulating agent and review his haemoglobin in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Erythropoiesis stimulating agents do have a role in lower risk myelodysplasia with a low endogenous erythropoietin level, but prescribing one before marrow diagnosis and risk stratification puts the treatment before the diagnosis. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis for an occult malignancy
options.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging is a reasonable search for marrow infiltration or occult malignancy, but the film already localises the problem to abnormal marrow production rather than to an external cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology

explanation.summary: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal stem cell disorders of older adults characterised by ineffective haematopoiesis, producing cytopenias despite a cellular marrow, with a variable risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia. The clue that separates dysplasia from the far commoner reversible causes of macrocytic anaemia is the blood film, where hypogranular neutrophils and bilobed pseudo Pelger-Huet forms, along with a reticulocyte response that is inadequate for the degree of anaemia, point to a production defect. Vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function, alcohol, liver disease and drugs must all be excluded first because they are common and treatable. Diagnosis requires marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics and increasingly with molecular panels, and treatment is directed by risk score: lower risk disease is managed with supportive care, erythropoiesis stimulating agents and sometimes lenalidomide, while higher risk disease is treated with hypomethylating agents or allogeneic transplantation in fitter patients. Isolated macrocytosis without anaemia in an older person is also worth investigating rather than dismissing.
key_points: Hypogranular and bilobed neutrophils on the film indicate dysplasia rather than a reversible macrocytic anaemia
Exclude vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, alcohol, liver disease and drugs first
A reticulocyte count that is not raised despite significant anaemia indicates a production defect
Marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics and molecular studies confirm the diagnosis and give the risk score
Treatment is risk-stratified, from supportive care in lower risk disease to hypomethylating agents or transplantation in higher risk disease
explanation.pearls: A serum erythropoietin level below 500 IU/L predicts response to erythropoiesis stimulating agents in lower risk myelodysplasia, so it is worth taking before any transfusion, since transfusion suppresses the endogenous level and makes the result uninterpretable.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes clinical practice resources

subtopic_detail: Investigating young onset hepatitis with a movement disorder and a low alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 22-year-old university student referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver tests found during an insurance medical.

Over the past 6 months his handwriting has become larger and untidy and his housemates have noticed his hands shake when he holds a cup. He has also become withdrawn and has failed a semester after previously passing comfortably. He denies alcohol beyond two drinks a month and takes no paracetamol, supplements or recreational drugs.

His alanine aminotransferase is 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20) and international normalised ratio 1.1. Hepatitis B and C serology are negative, autoimmune liver serology is negative, ferritin and transferrin saturation are within normal limits, and alpha-1 antitrypsin is normal.

His haemoglobin is 108 g/L (130-180) with a direct antiglobulin test that is negative. On examination he has a coarse postural tremor of both arms and mildly slurred speech, with no rigidity and normal power.

data_table.Examination: Coarse postural tremor of both arms, mildly slurred speech, no rigidity, normal power and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.1, haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-180), direct antiglobulin test negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, autoimmune liver serology negative, iron studies and alpha-1 antitrypsin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Liver biopsy with histological staging and quantitative tissue iron measurement
options.rationale: Biopsy with quantitative metal measurement can be informative but is invasive and would be arranged only after non-invasive testing is equivocal; iron studies are already normal, so measuring tissue iron answers the wrong question. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with susceptibility weighted sequences performed first
options.rationale: Brain imaging can show basal ganglia changes and supports the diagnosis, but it is not the confirmatory test and is arranged alongside or after the biochemical assessment rather than in place of it. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.text: Repeat autoimmune liver serology with immunoglobulin subclasses and coeliac antibodies
options.rationale: Repeating a negative autoimmune panel is unlikely to change the answer and does not explain the neurological signs, the anaemia with a negative direct antiglobulin test, or the low alkaline phosphatase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: Serum copper level alone, with a repeat measurement in 4 weeks for confirmation
options.rationale: Total serum copper largely reflects the copper bound to caeruloplasmin, so it falls as caeruloplasmin falls and can appear normal despite a high free copper fraction; it is not a useful standalone test. This is the near-pair to distinguish from caeruloplasmin and urinary copper. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.text: Serum caeruloplasmin with a 24 hour urinary copper collection and slit lamp examination
options.rationale: Hepatitis with a movement disorder and a psychiatric or academic decline in a young adult, alongside Coombs negative anaemia and a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase, is the combination that points to Wilson disease, and the diagnosis is built from a low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and Kayser-Fleischer rings. No single one of these is sufficient alone, which is why they are requested together. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources
Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by ATP7B mutations, in which copper accumulates in the liver and then spills into other tissues, notably the basal ganglia and cornea. It should be considered in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, particularly when neurological or psychiatric features accompany it, because the neurological form is frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder for years. No single test is diagnostic: caeruloplasmin is low in most but not all patients and is an acute phase reactant that can be falsely normal, urinary copper is raised, and Kayser-Fleischer rings are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement but in only about half of those presenting with liver disease alone. Two supporting clues are Coombs negative haemolytic anaemia from copper release and a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase. Treatment with chelation using penicillamine or trientine, or with zinc to block absorption, is lifelong and highly effective if started before irreversible damage, and first-degree relatives require screening.
key_points: Consider Wilson disease in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, especially with neurological or psychiatric features
Diagnosis combines low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and slit lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings
Total serum copper is unhelpful alone because it tracks caeruloplasmin
Coombs negative haemolysis and a low alkaline phosphatase are supportive clues
Treatment is lifelong chelation or zinc, and first-degree relatives must be screened
explanation.pearls: A ratio of alkaline phosphatase to total bilirubin below 4 in acute liver failure is highly suggestive of Wilson disease and should prompt immediate transplant unit referral, since fulminant Wilsonian failure is almost always fatal without transplantation.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post exercise facilitation in a smoker
stem:
You are the neurology registrar seeing a 62-year-old man referred with 4 months of difficulty getting out of a low chair and climbing the stairs at home.

He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He also mentions a persistently dry mouth that has made him carry a water bottle everywhere, and erectile difficulty that began around the same time. He has lost 3 kg without trying.

He has no double vision, no drooping eyelids, no difficulty swallowing and no change to his speech, and his symptoms do not fluctuate through the day.

On examination hip flexion and shoulder abduction are both reduced. When he grips your hand and sustains the effort for 15 seconds, his grip strength improves. His knee reflexes are absent on first testing but become obtainable after he contracts the quadriceps for 15 seconds. Sensation is normal. His creatine kinase is within normal limits and his thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexion and shoulder abduction, grip improves after 15 seconds of sustained effort, knee reflexes absent initially but obtainable after sustained quadriceps contraction, normal sensation, no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request acetylcholine receptor antibodies and arrange computed tomography of the mediastinum
options.rationale: This is the workup for myasthenia gravis, which characteristically involves ocular and bulbar muscles, worsens with sustained effort rather than improving, and preserves reflexes; the thymus rather than the lung is the associated structure. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.text: Request voltage gated calcium channel antibodies and arrange computed tomography of the chest
options.rationale: Proximal weakness that improves with sustained effort, reflexes that return after contraction, and autonomic features such as dry mouth and erectile dysfunction describe Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, confirmed by antibodies to the presynaptic voltage gated calcium channel. About half of cases are paraneoplastic and almost always from small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is part of the same request in a heavy smoker. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Request nerve conduction studies with low frequency repetitive stimulation of a distal nerve
options.rationale: Low frequency repetitive stimulation at 2 to 3 Hz demonstrates the decrement of myasthenia gravis; the presynaptic disorder here requires high frequency stimulation or brief maximal voluntary contraction to show the characteristic post-exercise increment. The distinguishing feature is decrement versus increment. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.text: Arrange a muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy
options.rationale: Muscle biopsy investigates an inflammatory or metabolic myopathy, which a normal creatine kinase and the post-exercise facilitation of both power and reflexes make improbable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Start prednisolone 50 mg daily and review his proximal strength in the clinic in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Empirical immunosuppression before a diagnosis risks masking or delaying identification of an underlying malignancy, which is the priority in a 62-year-old smoker with this syndrome. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a disorder of the presynaptic neuromuscular junction caused by antibodies against voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantal release of acetylcholine. The clinical signature is the mirror image of myasthenia gravis: proximal lower limb weakness dominates, ocular and bulbar involvement is mild or absent, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and erectile dysfunction are common, and both power and reflexes improve transiently after sustained contraction as calcium accumulates in the nerve terminal. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, overwhelmingly associated with small cell lung cancer, and the neurological syndrome commonly precedes the radiological detection of the tumour by months, so surveillance imaging is repeated if the initial scan is clear. Treatment of the tumour often improves the neurological syndrome, and symptomatic treatment uses amifampridine to prolong nerve terminal depolarisation, with immunosuppression or immunoglobulin for more severe disease. Recognising the syndrome matters practically because these patients are exquisitely sensitive to neuromuscular blocking agents during anaesthesia.
key_points: Proximal weakness, autonomic features and areflexia that reverses after contraction distinguish it from myasthenia gravis
Antibodies to voltage gated calcium channels confirm the diagnosis
About half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is mandatory
Electrophysiology shows an increment after high frequency stimulation or brief maximal contraction, not a decrement
Patients are highly sensitive to neuromuscular blocking agents, which matters before any anaesthetic
explanation.pearls: If the initial chest computed tomography is clear in a smoker with confirmed Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeat imaging every 3 to 6 months for at least 2 years, since the neurological syndrome commonly precedes detectable small cell lung cancer.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources
